title: ACME DNS-01 by RFC 2136 dynamic update with a TSIG key
description:
Split out of bead mimid-e13m.8, which built the ACME core and
`dns = "hook"`. docs/design/frontend-auth.md §5.2 rank 2 names this as one
of three ways to write the DNS-01 TXT record: an RFC 2136 dynamic update
with a TSIG key, which BIND, Knot and PowerDNS all take.

WHY IT IS ITS OWN BEAD AND NOT A FLAG. This is a DNS wire-format
implementation, not a branch in the `acme` module:

- the UPDATE opcode and its sections (RFC 2136 §2): zone, prerequisite,
  update, additional, which is not the shape of a query;
- the TSIG record (RFC 8945): the key name, the algorithm name
  (hmac-sha256), the time signed and fudge, the MAC over the canonical
  form of the request plus the TSIG variables, and the error and other-data
  fields;
- the transport: UDP with a TCP fallback for anything that does not fit,
  or TCP throughout, which is simpler and is what an update of one TXT
  record can afford;
- removing the record again after the challenge, which the hook method
  leaves to the operator's script.

Nothing in the tree does DNS wire format today, so none of this can be
borrowed. Estimate 400 to 600 lines with tests.

CONFIGURATION, already sketched in §5.3:

    [tls.acme]
    dns = "rfc2136"
    rfc2136 = { server = "ns1.example.org:53", key_name = "...", key_file = "..." }

The key file holds the TSIG secret, so it is read like any other secret:
mode checked, never logged, and the secret redacted in Debug output
(AGENTS.md's "secrets never reach logs").

TESTS, OFFLINE. A fake authoritative server: bind a UDP and a TCP socket,
decode the UPDATE, verify the TSIG MAC with the same key, and answer
NOERROR. That is the only way to test this without a nameserver, and it
doubles as the proof that the MAC is computed over the right bytes --
which is the part most likely to be wrong, and the part a real nameserver
would reject with NOTAUTH rather than explain.

WORTH WEIGHING FIRST: an operator who runs their own nameserver can
already write a three-line hook that calls `nsupdate`, which is the same
protocol driven by a tool that is already installed and already correct.
This bead buys not needing that hook. Decide whether that is worth 400 to
600 lines of TSIG that mimid then owns and has to keep right.
